questions.title: Why is accessibility important for UI/UX in enterprise software? Give real use cases where it matters.
questions.description: Accessibility means that everyone can use the app, including people with disabilities: users who are blind or have low vision, color blindness, motor impairments that make a mouse hard to use, hearing impairments, or cognitive limitations, and also people with temporary limitations, like a broken arm. In enterprise software this matters for several reasons. Employees must be able to do their job with the company's tools; an inaccessible app can exclude someone from their work. Many countries have laws and regulations that require accessible software, especially for the public sector (for example the European Accessibility Act, EN 301 549, and Section 508 in the US, based on the WCAG guidelines), and SAP's products follow these standards, so apps built on them are expected to as well. And accessible design improves usability for everyone: clear labels, good contrast, keyboard shortcuts and predictable focus help power users and people in difficult conditions too. Real use cases: a blind accountant uses a screen reader to post invoices, so every field needs a label and every icon button a text; a warehouse worker with gloves, or an expert who enters hundreds of records, works with the keyboard only; a user with low vision uses zoom and a high-contrast theme; a color-blind manager must see overdue items not only as red, but also with an icon or a text. A good answer gives three kinds of reasons. Legal: WCAG 2.1 level AA is the technical standard the laws point to, SAP publishes accessibility conformance documentation (a VPAT) for its products, and large tenders (governments, banks, healthcare, universities) require it, so an inaccessible app can lose the deal before anyone looks at the features. Business: a company with 50,000 users has thousands who benefit, for example around 8% of men are color-blind; if the ERP app they must use all day is unusable for them, the company has an employment problem, not a software problem. And it makes the app better for everyone. More use cases: a warehouse worker with low vision runs the browser at 200% zoom, so the layout must not break; a clerk with a broken arm works keyboard-only for six weeks, so every dialog must be reachable and closable without a mouse; a technician in bright sunlight needs high contrast. The sentence that lands well: "Accessibility is not only about disability; it is about not assuming every user is sitting at a desk with a mouse, perfect eyesight and full attention."
keyPoints: Accessibility lets everyone use the app, including people with visual, motor, hearing or cognitive impairments.
Employees must be able to do their job with company tools.
Laws and standards require it (WCAG, EN 301 549, European Accessibility Act, Section 508).
It improves usability for all: labels, contrast, keyboard use, predictable focus.
Legal (WCAG 2.1 AA, VPAT in tenders), business (e.g. ~8% of men are color-blind), and better UX for everyone.

examples.title: Accessibility in everyday app details
examples.code:
<!-- an icon-only button needs a text for screen readers -->
<Button icon="sap-icon://delete" tooltip="{i18n>delete}" press=".onDelete" />

<!-- status is shown with text and icon, not only with color -->
<ObjectStatus text="{i18n>overdue}" state="Error" icon="sap-icon://alert" />

<!-- every input has a label -->
<Label text="{i18n>invoiceAmount}" labelFor="amountInput" />
<Input id="amountInput" value="{Amount}" />

questions.title: What is ARIA?
questions.description: ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications), a W3C standard often called WAI-ARIA, defines extra HTML attributes that describe the meaning and state of UI elements to assistive technologies like screen readers. Plain HTML has built-in meaning for a few elements (a button, a link, a checkbox), but modern apps build complex widgets, like trees, tabs, comboboxes, or tables, out of div and span elements, which say nothing to a screen reader. ARIA fills this gap with three kinds of attributes: roles say what an element is (role="button", "tab", "dialog", "grid", "navigation"), states say its current condition (aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-checked, aria-disabled, aria-invalid), and properties give extra information and relations (aria-label, aria-labelledby, aria-describedby, aria-required, aria-haspopup). The screen reader reads this information, like "Shipping address, edit, required, invalid entry". In SAPUI5, the standard controls write the correct ARIA roles, states and properties automatically in their renderers, so app developers mostly need to provide the content: labels and relations through properties and associations like labelFor, ariaLabelledBy and ariaDescribedBy. Custom controls must write ARIA themselves, for example with RenderManager.accessibilityState(). The first rule of ARIA is: use a native element or a standard control with the right meaning, and add ARIA only where needed; wrong ARIA is worse than none. Concrete examples of what standard controls do: sap.m.Button renders role="button", sap.m.Input sets aria-required when required="true", and a Dialog sets role="dialog" and manages the focus. The piece people forget is announcing dynamic changes: when a search updates a table, a sighted user sees it, but a screen reader user hears nothing unless you announce it, with sap/ui/core/InvisibleMessage (mode Polite waits for a pause; Assertive interrupts and is reserved for errors), which uses an ARIA live region (aria-live) under the hood.
keyPoints: ARIA (WAI-ARIA) adds attributes that describe UI elements to assistive technologies.
Roles (what it is), states (its condition, like aria-expanded), properties (labels, relations, like aria-labelledby).
UI5 standard controls render ARIA automatically; apps provide labels via labelFor, ariaLabelledBy, ariaDescribedBy.
Custom controls write ARIA themselves (rm.accessibilityState); wrong ARIA is worse than none.
Announce dynamic changes with InvisibleMessage (Polite; Assertive only for errors).

questions.title: What is the purpose of labeling and tooltips for accessibility?
questions.description: Every interactive element must have an accessible name, the text a screen reader announces for it, otherwise a blind user hears only "edit text" or "button" and does not know what it is for. For input fields, the standard way is a visible sap.m.Label connected with labelFor="inputId" (or placing them together in a Form, which connects them automatically); the label is then announced when the field gets focus, and clicking the label focuses the field. When there is no visible label, for example a search field in a toolbar or an icon-only button, the name must come from elsewhere: ariaLabelledBy can point to another text, and sap.ui.core.InvisibleText provides a text that is not shown but can be referenced for screen readers. ariaDescribedBy adds extra, less important information, like a hint or a format. Tooltips (the tooltip property) show a short text when the mouse hovers over an element. For icon-only buttons, a tooltip is required, and UI5 also uses it as the accessible name. But tooltips must not be the only place for important information: they are not shown on touch devices, keyboard and screen reader users may not get them reliably, and they disappear quickly. So: visible labels for fields, tooltips for icon-only controls, and never hide essential information in a tooltip only. labelFor does three things at once: it links the label to the input for screen readers, clicking the label focuses the input (important for users with limited motor control), and the required asterisk appears on the label when the input is required. An icon-only toolbar without tooltips is completely unusable with a screen reader, and it is one of the most common accessibility findings in UI5 apps. InvisibleText is rendered off-screen, not with display:none, because hidden elements are ignored by screen readers too. Practical rules: every text is translatable (a hard-coded English tooltip="Delete" is an accessibility bug in every other language), and do not repeat the visible text of a button in its tooltip, or the screen reader says it twice.
keyPoints: Every interactive element needs an accessible name, announced by screen readers.
Inputs: a visible Label with labelFor (or a Form that connects them).
No visible label: ariaLabelledBy with a text or an InvisibleText; ariaDescribedBy for extra hints.
Tooltips are required for icon-only buttons, but must never be the only source of important information.
labelFor: screen reader link + click focuses the input + required asterisk.
Translate tooltips; do not repeat a button's visible text in its tooltip.

examples.title: Labels, invisible texts, and tooltips
examples.code:
<Label text="{i18n>customerName}" labelFor="customerInput" required="true" />
<Input id="customerInput" value="{CustomerName}" ariaDescribedBy="customerHint" />
<Text id="customerHint" text="{i18n>customerNameHint}" />

<core:InvisibleText id="searchLabel" text="{i18n>searchOrders}" />
<SearchField ariaLabelledBy="searchLabel" />

<Button icon="sap-icon://edit" tooltip="{i18n>edit}" press=".onEdit" />

questions.title: How is keyboard handling implemented in SAPUI5, and how can you customize it for keyboard-only use?
questions.description: Users must be able to do everything with the keyboard alone. SAPUI5's standard controls already support this: Tab and Shift+Tab move between focusable controls in a logical order, Enter or Space activate buttons and links, arrow keys move inside composite controls like lists, tables, tab bars, and menus (using item navigation, so the whole list is one Tab stop and the arrow keys move inside it), Escape closes dialogs and popovers, F4 or Alt+Down opens value helps and dropdowns, and F6 / Shift+F6 jumps between main areas of the page. Dialogs keep the focus inside them while open, and return it to the opener when closed. For your own needs, there are several ways to customize. The tab order follows the order in the view, so arrange controls logically instead of forcing focus with tabindex. Use pseudo events, which UI5 maps from keyboard events, like onsapenter, onsapspace, onsapescape, onsapup or onsapdown, either in a custom control, or on any control from the outside with control.addEventDelegate({ onsapenter: handler }). Set the focus deliberately where it helps, for example the first field of a form with initialFocus on a Dialog, or focus() after an action. For app-wide shortcuts, like Ctrl+S for Save, use commands (sap.ui.core.CommandExecution), declared in the manifest. Always test the app with the keyboard only. Home and End move to the first and last item. A table with 200 rows is one tab stop, and you move inside it with the arrow keys; that is the ItemNavigation pattern (sap/ui/core/delegate/ItemNavigation), which a custom control should reuse instead of writing the loop itself, because it handles arrow keys, Home/End, focus memory and the tabindex management. A block of the page becomes an F6 fast-navigation group with the custom data key sap-ui-fastnavgroup (written to the DOM). The test that costs nothing: unplug the mouse and complete one full task. A dialog you cannot close, a button you cannot reach, or focus that disappears after an action is a real bug.
keyPoints: Standard controls support Tab, Enter/Space, arrow keys inside composites, Escape, F4, and F6 groups.
Dialogs keep focus inside and return it to the opener; the tab order follows the view order.
Customize with pseudo events (onsapenter, onsapescape...) via addEventDelegate, and deliberate focus (initialFocus, focus()).
App-wide shortcuts with commands (CommandExecution, declared in the manifest); test keyboard-only.
Reuse ItemNavigation in custom controls; mark F6 groups with the sap-ui-fastnavgroup custom data.
Free test: unplug the mouse and finish one complete task.

questions.title: What are the general accessibility recommendations from the SAPUI5 documentation?
questions.description: The SAPUI5 documentation gives a set of practical rules for app developers. Use standard controls wherever possible, because they already have keyboard support, ARIA, focus handling, and high-contrast theme support; custom controls must provide all of this themselves. Give every input a label (with labelFor, or inside a Form), and every icon-only control a tooltip; use InvisibleText and ariaLabelledBy where there is no visible label. Do not use color as the only way to show information: add a text or an icon, like a status text with its state. Structure the page with titles in a correct hierarchy (Title with level H1, H2...) and landmarks, so screen reader users can understand and jump through the layout. Keep all texts in i18n, use clear wording, and do not write texts into images. Support all themes, including the high-contrast black and white themes, by using theme parameters instead of fixed colors. Handle focus deliberately: set initial focus in dialogs, and move focus to the new content after navigation or important actions. Show validation errors with value states and messages that are announced. Support zoom and text resizing, without fixed pixel sizes. Finally, test: navigate with the keyboard only, use a screen reader, switch to a high-contrast theme, and run the accessibility rules of the UI5 Support Assistant. Some rules in more detail: keep the DOM order logical, because the tab order follows the DOM, not the visual layout; never use positive tabindex values; after deleting a row, put the focus somewhere sensible, not at the top of the page; support 200% zoom with rem instead of px, wrapping texts and no fixed heights; and support right-to-left with the Begin/End classes. Checks in increasing cost: the URL parameters ?sap-ui-rtl=true and ?sap-ui-theme=sap_horizon_hcb (two minutes), browser zoom to 200%, a keyboard-only run-through of one task, the Support Assistant (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+S) accessibility rules, and a screen reader (NVDA on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS) for the critical screens. The closing thought: most accessibility problems in UI5 apps are not framework problems; they are missing labels, missing tooltips, color used alone, and custom controls without keyboard support, all cheap to fix while writing the code and expensive afterwards.
keyPoints: Use standard controls; they bring keyboard, ARIA, focus, and theme support.
Labels for inputs, tooltips for icon-only controls; never color alone to convey information.
Correct title hierarchy and landmarks; all texts in i18n; theme parameters so high-contrast themes work.
Deliberate focus handling, announced validation, zoom support; test with keyboard, screen reader, high contrast, Support Assistant.
No positive tabindex; logical DOM order; sensible focus after delete; 200% zoom with rem.
Cheap checks first: ?sap-ui-rtl=true, ?sap-ui-theme=sap_horizon_hcb, 200% zoom, keyboard-only, then Support Assistant and NVDA/VoiceOver.

examples.title: Title hierarchy and non-color status
examples.code:
<Page title="{i18n>orders}">
  <Title text="{i18n>openOrders}" level="H2" />
  <List items="{/Orders}">
    <ObjectListItem title="{OrderID}">
      <firstStatus>
        <ObjectStatus text="{StatusText}" state="{StatusState}" icon="{StatusIcon}" />
      </firstStatus>
    </ObjectListItem>
  </List>
</Page>
